I play a few sandboxes (e.g. SimCity, The Sims) with no main storyline (but a loveable world), and a few linear games with no openness to their loveable worlds (e.g. Dishonored). I play a lot of open world games where you are expected to use exploration and side missions to grind up your in-game numbers and real-world twitch reflexes so that you can beat the main storyline. In an open world game, I usually want to fall in love with the setting because I will have to pay a lot of attention to it.

Skyrim gave me many hours of escape. The first few hours were exhilarating and inspiring; I fell out of love when I noticed that I could investigate spells and alchemy but I just didn't respect the rules that governed them. Immersion flagged long before I had gotten to grips with the system. The main storyline was crap. The side quests and Dragonborn DLC were much more fun. I didn't give a damn about any of the humanoid characters: the setting was the only character I loved; the setting was beautiful and detailed and fascinating. Even if you want to be an alchemical wizard and you hate the magic and alchemy system, the lands of Skyrim and Solstheim are beautiful places in which to wander, especially if you can slow time with a shout and crush those who attack you. Even if you hate the available magic spells and potions, you can still appreciate the visual beauty of dwarven ruins and vampire afterlife realms. Fortunately it was possible to wander around even after the main quest had ended. Mods were a mixed blessing. The original game design was weak in terms of spell design and potion alchemy, but a customizable spell design system usually destroys so much challenge that the game becomes a tedious exercise.

Linear or open world or other doesn't really make the crucial difference. Any computer game MUST make me fall in love with the world above all else. (Assuming the gameplay is not tedious) I can be indifferent to the characters and the story so long as I love the world enough.

Fallout: New Vegas was mostly interesting as an exploration exercise. I wandered through most of the content. I didn't really "git gud." I mostly watched it like an entertaining movie. I really respected the writing of the main quest. I kept coming back to the DLC long after I had bored of the main quest, so the whole game managed to inspire me somehow. Again, I didn't care about the humanoid characters, I only loved the setting.

Fallout 4 gave me a few hours of distraction, but if New Vegas was an intellectual movie created by a solitary genius auteur, Fallout 4 was the schlocky imitation designed by a committee. There were some amazing ideas in Fallout 4, all of them half-formed and half-executed. If the setting was a character, it did not manage to get me to love it. After beating the main storyline, appreciating the writing of the Far Harbor DLC, and experimenting with a few mods, I didn't spend much more time on it. It was certainly not the worst open world game to attempt base building; I think Far Cry: New Dawn is worse than Fallout 4.

Elex was not engaging. I could tell the writers were intelligent, but I didn't enjoy the gameplay enough to spend more than a few hours in their world. I might have loved the setting if I had not been bored by the gameplay.

Just Cause 3 was nearly all core gameplay (maneuver, destroy, evade death, run around some more) and that was fun. The plot was an afterthought and I abandoned it when the special challenge missions became too tedious for me to "git gud." The setting was as thin as a Kleenex tissue; it was not a character.

Saints Row IV has some really annoying instant death traps in the last mission, and I doubt I will finish it, even if it would allow me to run around the main simulation world freely afterward. I respected the human characters; I felt little or nothing for the main world. For twenty-five hours it was mostly fun, and I had some respect for the intelligent comedy and style, but the final mission was damn tedious; I had no respect for the gameplay challenge design. I have not uninstalled it yet, but the tedium of dying over and over again seems to be reducing any desire I have to restart the game and "git gud."

It is not always the case that the core open world gameplay is more engaging that the main quest. Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon was an awesome seven hour nostalgia trip thoroughly suffused with enjoyable self-mocking humor (even though I never managed to correctly execute the shuriken takedown). Even though I loved the human characters and the setting, the experience is all about the main quest. The side missions are just little warm-up exercises in shooting some bad guys. The main quest is one of those rare, beautiful comedy action games. There are not many such games; No One Lives Forever is a non-open-world variant of the funny game that leverages nostalgia and wonderful art direction, but I can't think of many other such games.

In the end, I can tolerate a lot of different kinds of gameplay, so long as I get to spend time in a world that I love. I can tolerate mediocrity in rule design, gameplay, characters, and plot, so long as I somehow fall in love with the game world.
Do open world main storylines usually suck more than the core gameplay? Or am I the only one who needs stories to be set in worlds that I love?

Games that try to be "everything" usually fail. Open world games tend to have junk mechanics, combat is simplistic and becomes boring. I think the problem is trying to reach as big an audience as possible. The more you make something have mass appeal, the more it becomes a gray mass of rehashed concepts.

Take ice cream for example. If you were having a party and wanted everyone to get ice cream what flavor would you choose? Right off the bat you can exclude ones that people have allergies to. Then you can remove some of the more basic flavors that some people don't enjoy. Eventually you'll come to the conclusion that only chocolate and vanilla will satisfy the most people without excluding people. So it is with games. The more a game works toward mass appeal, the less it has any defining character.

Sandboxes that are primarily simulations don't need a story as you pointed out with SimCity. You can of course create custom maps and having a goal for the player to reach. SimCity 2000 did that with a couple of scenarios. You could string them together to make a "campaign" but often those are also tutorials that limit your options in each mission. Often I get bored in a sandbox game without a clear goal and stop playing once I have a stable or sustainable company, city, whatever.

Open world games are a bit different. They usually do have a central story and sometimes a way to keep the player heading in the right direction. They do need either the story to interest you so you play though it or they need an enjoyable world to keep you playing in it. The only ones I've played similar to your main examples are GTA3, Vice City, and San Andreas. I usually didn't care that much about the stories but you did have to play though them to unlock more of the map. The worlds were usually great though. I guess I played Oblivion, Morrowind (a little), and Daggerfall (only recently) but never finished the story of any of them.

Going back to your original question "Do open world main storylines usually suck more than the core gameplay?" I would say yes.

It all depends on tastes a lot ... I have played open world games that outclassed some other linear storyline based narrative games several times, even in story department. Some of those examples are Witcher III and STALKER games.

The best usually comes from mods, too. If there are big mods for games, then those games usually overgrow with time into something completely different and drastically better than vanilla, even if vanilla game is great.
